questions.question: What is the distribution of a random variable $X$?
options: The sample space before any random variable is defined, rather than the distribution
The largest value that $X$ can take
The probability measure on $\mathbb R$ assigning $P(X\in B)$ to suitable sets $B$
The single most likely value of $X$

questions.question: What does a distribution describe?
options: Where a random variable's probability lies.
Only the name of the sample space
The ordering of all outcomes
The number of variables in a dataset.

questions.question: What probability appears for the distribution of $X$?
options: $P(B\in X)$
$P(X\in B)$

questions.question: What uniquely determines the distribution of a real-valued random variable?
options: Its CDF
Its largest observed value only
The name of the variable
The number of prerequisites

questions.question: Can different random variables have the same distribution?
options: No, never
Only if they are the same function
Only if all probabilities are zero
Yes

questions.question: Two independent fair coin indicators both take values $0$ and $1$ with the same probabilities. What can be true?
options: Same Bernoulli distribution, but not the same random variable.
They must be the same function on the same outcome.
They cannot both be random variables
They have no distribution

questions.question: What does the distribution of a delivery time describe?
options: The exact name of the delivery driver only
The set of all events with no times
The probabilities of different time intervals
The probability that time is not numerical

questions.question: If $X$ is a die roll, what does $P(X\in\{2,4,6\})$ describe?
options: The distribution probability of an even die value
The probability of values outside the die support
The function value at the sample space
The probability that $X$ is not a random variable

questions.question: A mixture of customer types can create what kind of distributional shape?
options: A distribution with no probabilities
A sample space with no outcomes
A CDF that is decreasing
A distribution with several peaks

questions.question: If $B=[0,10]$, what does $P(X\in B)$ mean?
options: The probability that $X$ takes a value between $0$ and $10$
The probability that the sample space equals $[0,10]$
The probability that $B$ is a random variable
The probability that $X$ is outside every range

questions.question: Why is the distribution not necessarily the same as the random variable?
options: A random variable is a function; the distribution is its law.
The distribution is always an event in $S$
The random variable must be a probability measure.
They are identical whenever $X$ is real-valued

questions.question: How are discrete, continuous, and mixed distributions different?
options: They are all identical to the same CDF
They apply only to non-random variables
They allocate probability in different ways
They all assign mass to exactly one value

questions.question: Why does the definition use suitable sets $B$ rather than only single numbers?
options: Single numbers cannot be values of random variables.
The sample space must be a singleton
Events cannot be generated by intervals
Distributions assign probabilities to sets, not just single values.

questions.question: If $X$ and $Y$ have the same distribution, what must be true?
options: $X$ and $Y$ are the same function on every outcome
$P(X\in B)=P(Y\in B)$ for suitable value sets $B$
$X+Y=0$ always
$X$ and $Y$ have no CDF

questions.question: If a delivery-time distribution assigns high probability to $[0,2]$ hours, what does that mean?
options: The random variable cannot exceed $2$ hours
The sample space is exactly $[0,2]$
Short delivery times are likely under the model
The distribution has no support

questions.question: If two variables are different but both are fair coin indicators, what shared distribution do they have?
options: Uniform on all real numbers
Exponential on nonnegative times
Bernoulli with mass on $0$ and $1$
Poisson on all integers

questions.question: Why does the CDF uniquely determining the distribution matter?
options: It means two variables with the same CDF must be equal as functions
It means the sample space is no longer needed for modeling
It means all probabilities about value ranges are encoded by one function
It means all distributions are discrete

questions.question: Two distributions can share the same support but assign different probabilities. Which distinction does this reveal?
options: Support says where; distribution says how much.
Support gives all probabilities exactly
Distribution only lists impossible values.
They are always the same object

questions.question: If $X$ has the same distribution as $Y$, can observing $X$ and observing $Y$ still be different experiments?
options: Yes; same distribution need not mean the same random variable.
No, same distribution makes them the same function.
No, same distribution removes randomness
Yes, but only if both have probability zero

questions.question: A population combines business and leisure customers with different spending patterns. What concept describes the resulting spending law?
options: A single generated event only
A mixture distribution
A probability axiom
A support with no distribution
